strategy.title: No plan: the $5,000 figure is a state grant award, not a price buyers pay
strategy.why: The only opening (dementia-care training workbook for assisted living facilities) has a reachable register of 410 administrators, a dated signal, a measured 5-of-120 acceptance rate, Brain fulfilment and $20 cost, but its only 'price' is the Department of Aging grant of $5,000 awarded to a facility that completes an approved program. A grant to the facility is not what a facility pays for a workbook, so no purchase price is evidenced and the deals needed for $5,000 are undetermined.

alternatives.why: The grant is paid by the state to facilities for completing an approved program; it says nothing about what an administrator will pay a vendor, nor that this workbook is an approved program.

openings.title: Dementia-care staff training curriculum workbook for assisted living facilities

card.reachableChannel: Administrator emails from the state's licensed assisted-living facility register
card.offerScope: Dementia-care staff training curriculum workbook for assisted living facilities

links.basis: reach: Administrator emails from the state's licensed assisted-living facility register
no single price on the card
measured on this offer's own sales: 5 accepted of 120 contacts
a one-off needs its one buyer
7 days to usable cash against 30 left

facts.value: The state register lists 410 licensed assisted living facilities, each with a named administrator.
Sell Dementia-care staff training curriculum workbook for assisted living facilities to each buyer.
The state Department of Aging's Dementia Care Training Grant awards $5,000 to each licensed facility that completes an approved staff training program (program notice, 2026-10).

reviews.reasons: NO_PLAN is right and names the decisive gap. The card's only price is the Department of Aging Dementia Care Training Grant ($5,000 awarded by the state to a facility that completes an approved program, notice 2026-10): that is a grant to the facility, not a price an administrator pays a vendor, and nothing shows this workbook is an approved program; the author correctly marks it matchesBuyer false and refuses to count it. With no purchase price, revenue per deal is unknown; the conversion fact (5 agreements from 120 contacts) states no price, so it cannot be read as a price either. Recomputed bounds so the gap is decisive: at the measured 4.2% over all 410 registered facilities about 17 deals are reachable in the window, so $5,000 needs at least ~$295 per deal - a figure no record supports; nor does any record support a single $5,000 sale. Other links hold (register of 410 administrators, dated signal, Brain produces the workbook, $20 cost, $0 exposure, 7-day settlement). No constraint is claimed, which is correct: the gap is missing evidence, not a limit the evidence cannot fit.
findings: Resolution: 'published prices for dementia-care curricula' are other vendors' benchmarks and would not establish what these administrators pay; the decisive evidence is written, money-committed acceptances at a stated price from the register (or the price on the 5 recorded agreements, if they had one). Lead with that.

State the threshold the live offer must clear: with ~17 reachable deals at 4.2%, a price of at least ~$300 (or fewer deals at a higher price) is needed for $5,000; a lower evidenced price makes the target unreachable in this window.
If the workbook could qualify as an approved program under the grant, that would be a different, unevidenced mechanism; it is correctly not assumed.
